[[File:2. Quota reform movement 2024 in Bangladesh.jpg|thumb|[[Bangladesh]]'s [[July Uprising|Student–People's uprising]] of 2024 has been dubbed the world's first successful [[Generation Z]]–led revolution, ending [[Sheikh Hasina]]'s 15-year-long autocratic rule. ]][[Generation Z]] (or Gen Z), colloquially referred to as "zoomers" in [[Western world|the West]],<ref name="Wordswatching2">{{Cite web |date=January 13, 2020 |title=Words We're Watching: 'Zoomer' |url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/words-at-play/words-were-watching-zoomer-gen-z |access-date=January 30, 2020 |website=Merriam-Webster}}</ref><ref name="zoomer Dictionary.com">{{Cite web |date=January 16, 2020 |title=zoomer |url=https://www.dictionary.com/e/slang/zoomer/ |access-date=14 June 2020 |website=Dictionary.com}}</ref> is the demographic [[Cohort (statistics)|cohort]] succeeding [[Millennials]] and preceding [[Generation Alpha]].<ref name=":110">{{Cite news |last=Williams |first=Alex |date=September 19, 2015 |title=Meet Alpha: The Next 'Next Generation' |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/09/19/fashion/meet-alpha-the-next-next-generation.html |access-date=September 7, 2019 |work=The New York Times |department=Fashion}}</ref> Researchers and popular media use the mid-to-late 1990s as starting birth years and the early 2010s as ending birth years, with the generation generally being defined as people born from 1997 to 2012.<ref>{{Cite news |last=June |first=Sophia |date=2021-07-10 |title=Could Gen Z Free the World From Email? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/07/10/business/gen-z-email.html |access-date=2021-07-10 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

In the late 2010s, Generation Z was often portrayed as a [[Progressivism|progressive]] cohort, showing strong support for social issues, such as [[climate change mitigation]].<ref name=":60">{{Cite web |date=2019-01-17 |title=Generation Z Looks a Lot Like Millennials on Key Social and Political Issues |url=http://www.pewsocialtrends.org/2019/01/17/generation-z-looks-a-lot-like-millennials-on-key-social-and-political-issues/ |access-date=November 22, 2019 |website=Pew Research Center |language=en-US}}</ref> The generation has been described as "pro-government."<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=2020-05-14 |title=What We Know About Gen Z So Far |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2020/05/14/on-the-cusp-of-adulthood-and-facing-an-uncertain-future-what-we-know-about-gen-z-so-far-2/ |access-date=2021-06-24 |website=Pew Research Center’s Social & Demographic Trends Project |language=en-US}}</ref>

This perception has been challenged in Europe<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-03-17 |title=Europe's far right uses TikTok to win youth vote |url=https://www.politico.eu/article/tiktok-far-right-european-parliament-politics-europe/ |access-date=2025-10-15 |website=Politico |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-06-06 |title=Nigel Farage surges with Gen Z women |url=https://www.politico.eu/article/nigel-farage-reform-uk-polls-gen-z-women-populist-elections-conservatives-labour-brexit-tiktok-dei-housing/ |access-date=2025-10-15 |website=Politico |language=en-GB}}</ref> and the United States<ref>{{Cite web |last=Berger |first=Chloe |date=November 7, 2024 |title=Trump's victory reveals secret Republicans: Joe Rogan-obsessed Gen Z men |url=https://fortune.com/2024/11/07/trumps-victory-reveals-secret-republicans-joe-rogan-obsessed-gen-z-men/ |website=Fortune}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Hill |first=Faith |date=November 14, 2024 |title=The Not-So-Woke Generation Z |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/family/archive/2024/11/gen-z-woke-myth-election/680653/ |website=[[The Atlantic]]}}</ref> where Gen Z voters have supported [[Right-wing populism|right-wing populist]] parties as well as [[Left-wing populism|left-wing populist]] parties.<ref>{{Cite web |last=with |first=An interview |title=What Populism Can (and Can't) Do for the Left |url=https://jacobin.com/2025/10/populism-class-parties-democrats-mamdani |access-date=2025-10-15 |website=jacobin.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ward |first=Bradley |last2=Guglielmo |first2=Marco |title=People, class, democracy: re-mapping left populism from populist social democracy to popular socialism |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/13569317.2024.2371506 |journal=Journal of Political Ideologies |volume=0 |issue=0 |pages=1–22 |doi=10.1080/13569317.2024.2371506 |issn=1356-9317}}</ref> The political divide within Gen Z has become increasingly pronounced along gender lines in some countries.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Opinion {{!}} Why Generation Z Embraced Trump |url=https://www.wsj.com/opinion/why-generation-z-embraced-donald-trump-young-voters-election-99c59054 |date=2025-03-11|access-date=2025-04-16 |website=WSJ |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Penley |first=Taylor |date=2025-03-24 |title=Gen Z influencer uncovers the truth about young Americans' views on Trump |url=https://www.foxbusiness.com/media/gen-z-influencer-uncovers-truth-about-young-americans-views-trump |access-date=2025-04-16 |website=FOXBusiness |language=en-US}}</ref> According to ''[[Politico]]'', age may play a large role in political ideology of Gen Z depending on how young they were during world events such as the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]. Older members of Gen Z leaned progressive while younger members were more conservative, particularly in the United States.<ref>{{cite web|last=Janfaza|first=Rachel|date=26 April 2025|title=The New Partisan Divide Is Old Gen Z vs. Young Gen Z|work=Politico|url=https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2025/04/26/two-gen-zs-young-conservative-polling-00307375|access-date=29 April 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-04-27 |title=Young men and women are taking the 'gender gap' to staggering new levels |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/elections/young-men-women-are-taking-poll-gender-gap-staggering-new-levels-rcna202672 |access-date=2025-04-29 |website=NBC News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Paz |first=Christian |date=2025-05-27 |title=There are two Gen Zs |url=https://www.vox.com/politics/414266/republican-conservative-two-gen-z-young-voter-trumpier-progressive |access-date=2025-06-01 |website=Vox |language=en-US}}</ref>

Movements associated with Gen Z so far include [[fourth-wave feminism]], [[School Strike for Climate]], [[March for Our Lives]], [[Students Against Discrimination]] and [[Gaza war protests|Pro-Palestine movement]].<ref name="refinery29" /><ref name="BusinessInsiderClimate" /><ref>{{cite news |last=Karatas |first=Dilara |last2=Karadag |first2=Murat |last3=Pala |first3=Melike |title=Biggest student movement of 21st century: Pro‑Palestinian protests spread across global campuses |url=https://www.aa.com.tr/en/world/-biggest‑student‑movement‑of‑21st‑century‑pro‑palestinian‑protests‑spread‑across‑global‑campuses/3215689 |work=Anadolu Agency |date=10 May 2024}}</ref> [[Gen Z protests]] have [[Gen Z protests|toppled governments in Asia and Africa]], and are associated with [[internet activism]].

Contrary to older generations, who mainly receive news from [[News broadcasting|television news]], Generation Z receives their information predominantly from [[social media]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Taylor |first=Kate |title=Gen Z is more conservative than many realize — but the Instagram-fluent generation will revolutionize the right |date=1 July 2019 |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/gen-z-changes-political-divides-2019-7 |access-date=2021-06-25 |website=Business Insider |language=en}}</ref>

== Voting patterns ==
According to Sean Simpsons of [[Ipsos]], people are more likely to vote when they have more at stake, such as children to raise, homes to maintain, and income taxes to pay.<ref name=":82">{{Cite news |last=Dhaliwal |first=Taz |date=September 30, 2019 |title=For the 1st time, millennial voters will make up the biggest voting bloc in a federal election |url=https://globalnews.ca/news/5938985/millenials-biggest-voting-block-canada-election-2019/ |access-date=October 15, 2019 |work=Global News}}</ref> The generational gap of political positions could be due to the fact that today's youths grew up in different sociopolitical environments to their parents and grandparents - environments which make them more likely to go to [[university]], correlating with [[Social liberalism|socially liberal]] views on certain issues.<ref name=":55">{{Cite news |last=Tilley |first=James |date=October 4, 2015 |title=Hard Evidence: do we become more conservative with age? |url=https://theconversation.com/hard-evidence-do-we-become-more-conservative-with-age-47910 |access-date=November 16, 2020 |work=The Conversation}}</ref> Since Gen Z are the second generation to own less than their predecessors at the same age, after Millennials, [[economic redistribution|economically redistributive]] policies tend to be popular with the generation.

In recent years, a political gender gap between Gen Z men and women emerged, with Gen Z men leaning towards [[conservatism]] and [[right-wing populism]], and women leaning towards support for [[Liberalism|liberal]] policies and [[left-wing populism]], a gap that has been detected by various research and numerous countries, but more predominantly in [[Argentina]], [[Brazil]], the [[United States]] and [[South Korea]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/breaking-down-gender-gap-gen-z-politics-desk-rcna177155|title=Breaking down the yawning gender gap dividing Gen Z: From the Politics Desk|date=October 24, 2024|website=NBC News}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/17/learning/lesson-plans/lets-discuss-the-gender-gap-among-gen-z-voters.html | title=Let's Discuss: The Gender Gap Among Gen Z Voters | work=The New York Times | date=October 17, 2024 }}</ref>

=== Europe ===
In the [[2019 European Parliament election in France]], the support of the [[Far-right politics|far-right]] [[National Rally (France)|National Rally]] (formerly the National Front) among those 35 and under nearly halved as compared to the [[2014 European Parliament election in France|2014 election]], where the Front won the plurality of votes in that age group.<ref>{{Cite web |last=figaro |first=le |date=May 26, 2014 |title=Olivier, 19 ans: "J'ai voté FN et j'assume" |url=https://etudiant.lefigaro.fr/les-news/actu/detail/article/olivier-19-ans-j-ai-vote-fn-et-j-assume-5450/ |access-date=2021-06-25 |website=Le Figaro Etudiant |language=fr}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last1=de Weck |first1=Joseph |last2=Ferguson |first2=Niall |date=September 30, 2019 |title=European Millennials Are Not Like Their American Counterparts |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2019/09/europes-young-not-so-woke/598783/ |access-date=June 25, 2021 |website=The Atlantic}}</ref> Depending on how the generation is defined, the 2014 election either had one year or no years of Generation Z voters, while the 2019 election had four to six years. In the first round of the [[2017 French presidential election|2017 presidential election]], National Front candidate [[Marine Le Pen]] won more votes from people between the ages of 18 and 35 than any other candidate. Moreover, the share of women aged 18 to 26 who backed the [[Le Pen family|Le Pen political family]] rose from 9% in 1988 to 32% in 2017, closing the gender gap in the process.<ref name=":32">{{Cite book |last1=Eatwell |first1=Roger |author-link1=Roger Eatwell |title=National Populism - The Revolt Against Liberal Democracy |last2=Goodwin |first2=Matthew |author-link2=Matt Goodwin (author) |publisher=Pelican Book |year=2018 |isbn=978-0-241-31200-1 |location=Great Britain |chapter=Chapter 1: Myths}}</ref>

In Austria, more than one in two men between the ages of 18 and 29 voted for the [[Austrian nationalism|nationalist]] [[Freedom Party of Austria|Freedom Party]] in the [[2016 Austrian presidential election|2016 presidential election]], and 30% of those ages 18 to 29 voted for the Freedom Party in the [[2017 Austrian legislative election|2017 parliamentary elections]].<ref name=":32" /> However, in the [[2019 European Parliament election in Austria|2019 European Parliament election]], the Freedom Party came in third with the same age group (17%), behind both [[The Greens – The Green Alternative|the Greens]] (28%) and the [[Social Democratic Party of Austria|Social Democratic Party]] (22%).

In the [[2019 European Parliament election in Germany]], 30% of voters aged 18 to 30 voted for the [[European Green Party|Green Party]], beating every other political party by wide margins in that particular age group.<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 27, 2019 |title=Infographic: How German youth voted in the European Elections |url=https://www.statista.com/chart/18170/voting-results-of-germans-aged-30-or-below-at-the-european-elections/ |access-date=2021-06-25 |website=Statista Infographics |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":6" />

In Italy, the [[populist]] party [[Five Star Movement]] won the youth vote overwhelmingly in the [[2018 Italian general election|2018 national election]]. But in the [[2019 European Parliament election in Italy|2019 European Parliament election]], the [[Right-wing politics|right-wing]] party [[Lega Nord]] won the largest vote-share among both millennials and Gen Z.<ref name=":6" />

In the [[2019 European Parliament election in Poland]], the [[National conservatism|national-conservative]] [[Law and Justice (Poland)|Law and Justice party]] came first among those aged 18 to 29.<ref name=":6" />

In the 2022 school elections in [[Sweden]], in which 80% percent of all Swedish teenagers participated, 9% voted for [[Left-wing politics|left-wing]] parties, 21% voted for [[Centre-left politics|centre-left]] parties, 8% voted for a [[Centrism|centrist]] party, 41% voted for [[Centre-right politics|centre-right]] parties, and 21% voted for a right-wing party.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Resultat i Skolval 2022 {{!}} MUCF |url=https://www.mucf.se/resultat-i-skolval-2022 |access-date=2023-12-25 |website=www.mucf.se |language=sv}}</ref>

Political scientist George Tilley notes that, in the United Kingdom, while older people tend to vote for the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]], young people tend to choose the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]], the [[Liberal Democrats (UK)|Liberal Democrats]], or the [[Green Party of England and Wales|Green Party]].<ref name=":55" /> In the [[2019 United Kingdom general election|2019 UK general election]], the Labour Party had a 43-point lead over the Conservative Party among voters aged 18 to 24.<ref>{{Cite web |title=IPSOS MORI: How the voters voted in the 2019 election |url=https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2019-12/general-election-2019-poll-aggregate-v8.pdf |access-date=July 31, 2022 |website=IPSOS}}</ref> Winning the support of young people does not necessarily translate to increasing young voters' turnouts in the UK,<ref name=":19">{{Cite news |date=January 29, 2018 |title=The myth of the 2017 'youthquake' election |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-politics-42747342 |access-date=December 15, 2019 |work=BBC News |department=UK}}</ref> and positive reactions on social media may not lead to success at the ballot box.<ref name=":20">{{Cite news |last=Sopel |first=Jon |date=December 15, 2019 |title=Will UK provide light bulb moment for US Democrats? |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-50785442 |access-date=December 15, 2019 |work=BBC News |department=US & Canada}}</ref>  Despite reports of a surge in turnouts among young voters in the [[2015 United Kingdom general election|2015]] and [[2017 United Kingdom general election|2017]] United Kingdom general elections, statistical scrutiny by the [[British Election Study|British Elections Study]] revealed that the margin of error was too large to determine whether or not there was a significant increase or decrease in the number of young participants. In both cases, turnouts among those aged 18 to 24 was between 40% and 50%.

Ahead of the [[2025 German federal election]], the left-wing party [[Die Linke|The Left]] saw a surge amongst younger voters in the last days before the election, and eventually, came first amongst 18-24 year old voters with 25% of the vote. The right-wing populist [[Alternative for Germany]] came second amongst the age group with 21% of the vote, stronger than with over 60-year olds.<ref>{{Cite web |last=mdr.de |title=Interaktive Grafik zur Bundestagswahl: Alter, Bildung, Geschlecht – wer wählte wen? {{!}} MDR.DE |url=https://www.mdr.de/nachrichten/deutschland/politik/bundestagswahl-wer-waehlte-wen-100.html |access-date=2025-08-24 |website=www.mdr.de |language=de}}</ref> Amongst the 18-24 year olds, also a gender gap was visible, with 35% of women aged 18 to 24 voting for Die Linke and overall 60% of young women voting for left-wing parties (The Left, [[Social Democratic Party of Germany|Social Democratic Party]], [[Alliance 90/The Greens|The Greens]]), whilst amongst 18-24-year-old men, Alternative for Germany came first with 27% of the vote and about 50% of men voting for right-wing parties (also including [[Christian Democratic Union of Germany|Christian Democratic Union]] and classical liberal [[Free Democratic Party (Germany)|Free Democratic Party]]).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sonnenberg |first=Peter |title=Wodurch das Wahlverhalten junger Menschen beeinflusst wird |url=https://www.tagesschau.de/inland/bundestagswahl/junge-waehler-motivation-100.html |access-date=2025-08-24 |website=tagesschau.de |language=de}}</ref>

=== Americas ===
====United States====
{{See also|Youth vote in the United States}}

In a 2016 mock election of upper elementary, middle, and high school students conducted by [[Houghton Mifflin Harcourt]], [[Hillary Clinton]] beat [[Donald Trump]] among the students, with Clinton receiving 46% of the vote, Donald Trump receiving 41%, and other candidates receiving 12%.<ref>{{Cite news |title=America's Youth Have Spoken: Hillary Clinton Is Generation Z's Choice for President |url=http://www.hmhco.com/media-center/press-releases/2016/october/one-vote-2016-results |access-date=26 February 2017}}</ref> A 2017 survey produced by [[MTV]] and the [[Public Religion Research Institute]] found that 72% of Americans aged 15 to 24 held unfavorable views of President Donald Trump.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Vandermaas-Peeler |first1=Alex |last2=Cox |first2=Daniel |last3=Fisch-Friedman |first3=Molly |last4=Jones |first4=Robert P. |date=10 January 2018 |title=Diversity, Division, Discrimination: The State of Young America {{!}} MTV/PRRI Report |url=https://www.prri.org/research/mtv-culture-and-religion/ |access-date=18 March 2018 |publisher=[[Public Religion Research Institute]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Scott |first=Eugene |date=11 January 2018 |title=The state of America, according to Generation Z |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/the-fix/wp/2018/01/11/the-state-of-america-according-to-generation-z/ |access-date=18 March 2018 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]}}</ref> A 2018 [[Pew Research Center]] poll found that among those aged 13 to 21, only 30% approved of Trump's job performance,<ref name=":60" /> and in a 2020 Politico poll, only about 28% of those aged 18 to 23 approved of Donald Trump's job performance.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=6 things to know about Gen Z, politics and 2020 |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2020/10/11/gen-z-politics-2020-poll-takeaways-426767 |access-date=2021-06-22 |website=Politico |date=October 11, 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

In the [[2018 United States elections|2018 midterm elections]], voter turnout among 18 to 29-year-olds went up to 36% from 20% in [[2014 United States elections|2014]], the largest percentage point increase for any age group.<ref>{{Cite web |publisher=United States Census Bureau |title=Behind the 2018 U.S. Midterm Election Turnout |url=https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2019/04/behind-2018-united-states-midterm-election-turnout.html |access-date=2021-06-26 |website=The United States Census Bureau |language=EN-US}}</ref> This increase in youth turnout has been attributed to a rebuttal of Trump among young millennials and older members of Generation Z, as well as to the [[Get out the vote|get out the vote initiatives]] that were part of the student-led [[2018 United States gun violence protests|gun violence protest]] [[March for Our Lives]], which was described as "Generation Z's first social movement".<ref name="refinery29">{{Cite web |last=Gontcharova |first=Natalie |title=The Verdict Is In: The Youth Vote Shaped The Midterm Results |url=https://www.refinery29.com/en-us/2018/11/216416/youth-vote-turnout-midterm-election-results |access-date=2021-06-26 |website=www.refinery29.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Hansen |first=Claire |date=November 7, 2018 |title=Young Voters Turned Out in Historic Numbers, Early Estimates Show |url=https://www.usnews.com/news/politics/articles/2018-11-07/young-voters-turned-out-in-historic-numbers-early-estimates-show |website=US News}}</ref> However, according to a field survey by ''The'' ''Washington Post'' interviewing every fifth person at the protest, only ten percent of the participants were 18 years of age or younger. Meanwhile, the adult participants of the protest had an average age of just under 49.<ref name=":212">{{Cite news |last=Fisher |first=Dana |date=28 March 2018 |title=Here's who actually attended the March for Our Lives. (No, it wasn't mostly young people.) |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/monkey-cage/wp/2018/03/28/heres-who-actually-attended-the-march-for-our-lives-no-it-wasnt-mostly-young-people |access-date=20 January 2019 |newspaper=Washington Post}}</ref>

According to a Politico survey, a [[2020 United States presidential election|2020 presidential election]] with only Generation Z voters would see [[Joe Biden]] win 51% of the popular vote, compared to Donald Trump's 25%. However, almost half of Biden voters said they were voting ''against'' Trump rather than ''for'' Biden, reflected in lower approval ratings for both Joe Biden and congressional [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] than the general public.<ref name=":2" /> In the 2020 presidential election, 50% of those aged 18 to 29 voted, compared to 39% in the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 election]]. In addition, voter turnout among newly eligible voters (ages 18 and 19) was 46%, stronger than previous years. The increase has also been attributed to [[Postal voting in the United States#Expansion in 2020 election|the expansion of postal voting]] due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |date=April 29, 2021 |title=Half of Youth Voted in 2020, An 11-Point Increase from 2016 |url=https://circle.tufts.edu/latest-research/half-youth-voted-2020-11-point-increase-2016 |access-date=2021-06-25 |website=circle.tufts.edu |language=en}}</ref>

Representative [[Maxwell Frost]] (born in 1997) has become the first and only member of Generation Z so far to be elected into the United States Congress.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Liu |first=Jennifer |date=November 9, 2022 |title=25-year-old Maxwell Frost will be the first Gen Z member of Congress |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/11/09/maxwell-frost-will-be-the-first-gen-z-member-of-congress.html |access-date=12 November 2022 |website=CNBC |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Moore |first=Elena |date=8 November 2022 |title=Maxwell Frost elected as the first Gen Z member of Congress |url=https://www.npr.org/2022/11/08/1134743908/maxwell-frost-calvin-wimbish-florida-10th-house-midterms-results |website=NPR |language=en}}</ref> He ran for [[Florida's 10th congressional district]] representing the Democratic Party.

In the 2024 U.S. election, Gen Z voters displayed notable gender-based differences in their voting patterns. Gen Z women, more than men, tended to support progressive candidates, influenced by concerns about issues like [[reproductive rights]], [[LGBTQ rights in the United States|LGBTQ+ rights]],  and [[Fourth-wave feminism]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-10-24 |title=Breaking down the yawning gender gap dividing Gen Z: From the Politics Desk |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/breaking-down-gender-gap-gen-z-politics-desk-rcna177155 |access-date=2024-12-03 |website=NBC News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Janfaza |first=Rachel |date=2024-11-08 |title=Here's the Breakdown of How Young People Actually Voted in 2024 |url=https://www.teenvogue.com/story/youth-vote-in-2024-young-men-trump-women-of-color-harris |access-date=2024-12-03 |website=Teen Vogue |language=en-US}}</ref> This pattern was consistent with broader trends, where younger women were more likely to back [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] candidates. Meanwhile, Gen Z men shifted further to Republican candidates like Trump.<ref>{{Cite web |last=McLister |first=Frankie |date=2024-11-08 |title=Men of Gen Z backed Donald Trump, fueling his political comeback, polls say - CBS Minnesota |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/minnesota/news/young-men-donald-trump/ |access-date=2024-12-03 |website=www.cbsnews.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Trepany|first=Charles|date=2024-11-18 |title=The rise of Trump bros and why some Gen Z men are shifting right |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/life/health-wellness/2024/11/18/trump-gen-z-bros-maga-voters/76337571007/|newspaper=USA Today |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Penley |first=Taylor |date=2024-11-10 |title=Trump won over Gen Z men by being the 'assertive, outspoken' candidate they needed, YouTuber says |url=https://www.foxnews.com/media/trump-won-over-gen-z-men-being-assertive-outspoken-candidate-needed-youtuber-says |access-date=2024-12-03 |website=Fox News |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The Youth Vote in 2024 |url=https://circle.tufts.edu/2024-election |access-date=2025-08-24 |website=circle.tufts.edu |language=en}}</ref> Explanations for Trump's gains with young men include the economy, appealing to them through podcasters like [[Joe Rogan]], "speaking to" their mental health struggles, less outreach from liberals, and men feeling "left behind" amid progress for women.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jamelle |first=Bouie |title=Gender Gap in Voting 2024 |website=[[The New York Times]] |date=October 26, 2024 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/26/opinion/gender-election-voting-men-women-young.html}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Potas |first=Dace |title=Opinion: Turns out Gen Z wasn't completely sold on Harris. Men flocked to Trump. |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/opinion/columnist/2024/11/07/trump-win-men-gen-z-voted/76095027007/ |date=2024-11-07|access-date=2024-12-03 |website=USA TODAY |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/08/31/politics/video/smr-gender-gap-genz-voters |title=Widest Gender Gap among Gen-Z Voters {{!}} CNN Politics |date=2024-08-31 |last=Burns |first=Amelia |language=en |access-date=2024-12-03 |via=www.cnn.com}}</ref> Some post-election surveys of Gen Z voters have found their rightward shift in the 2024 election may have been temporary.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://thehill.com/opinion/campaign/5134296-gen-z-men-voting-trump/ |title=Gen Z men's rightward shift is happening, but could be temporary |date=2025-02-10 |last=Deckman |first=Melissa |access-date=2025-10-28 |website=The Hill}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.newsweek.com/gen-z-polling-democrats-trump-2103421 |title=Gen Z is Shifting Back Toward Democrats |date=2025-07-24 |last=McHardy |first=Martha |access-date=2025-10-28 |website=Newsweek}}</ref>

====South America====
In 2022, exit polls revealed that voters aged 18 to 24 intended to vote overwhelmingly (by a margin of over 35%) for [[Gustavo Petro]] in the [[Two-round system|runoff]] for the [[2022 Colombian presidential election|Colombian presidential election]].<ref name=":11">{{Cite news |last=Turkewitz |first=Julie |date=2022-06-19 |title=Colombia Presidential Election: Colombia Election: Gustavo Petro Makes History in Presidential Victory |url=https://www.nytimes.com/live/2022/06/19/world/colombia-election-results |access-date=2023-01-14 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Petro's victory marked the first time that a leftist politician was elected to the office.<ref name=":11" />

The same phenomenon was seen in the [[2022 Brazilian general election|2022 presidential election in Brazil]], where polls estimate that 51% of young voters between 16 and 24 years voted for the [[Workers' Party (Brazil)|Workers' Party]] candidate, [[Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva]], elected with 50.9% of the votes.{{Citation needed|date=January 2023}} The [[Socialism and Liberty Party|Socialism and Freedom Party]] (PSOL), that targets young voters from the middle class, was the fastest growing party in Brazil since 2017.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-04-30 |title=PSol cresce 48% no governo Bolsonaro, mas ainda é nanico frente ao PT {{!}} Metrópoles |url=https://www.metropoles.com/brasil/politica-brasil/psol-cresce-48-no-governo-bolsonaro-mas-ainda-e-nanico-frente-ao-pt |access-date=2023-01-14 |website=www.metropoles.com |language=pt-BR}}</ref>

Argentina, on the other hand, has seen an uprising of right-wing and pro-market movements in younger generations, as polls estimate that the majority of young voters between 16 and 24 years voted [[Javier Milei]] for president in the [[2023 Argentine general election]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 21, 2023 |title=Mapa &#124; ¿Quién ha votado a Milei? Así son sus apoyos por edad, género o territorio |url=https://elpais.com/argentina/2023-11-21/mapa-quien-ha-votado-a-milei-asi-son-sus-apoyos-por-edad-genero-o-territorio.html}}</ref>

== Social values ==

=== Family values and abortion ===
[[File:Youths'_Support_for_Safe_and_Legal_Abortion_(Varkey_2016).png|379x379px|right]]
A 2018 Pew Research Center survey studied various [[family values]] among generations. Among Generation Z, 67% were indifferent towards premarital cohabitation. 49% considered [[Single parent|single motherhood]] to be neither a positive or a negative for society. 62% saw increased ethnic or racial diversity as good for society and 53% for [[interracial marriage]]. In the case of financial responsibility in a two-parent household, majorities from across the generations (79% of Generation Z) answered that it should be shared by both parents. Across all the generations surveyed, at least 84% thought that both parents ought to be responsible for [[Parenting|rearing children]]. About 13% of Generation Z thought that mothers should be the primary caretaker of children, while very few thought that fathers should be the ones mainly responsible.<ref name=":60" />

In 2016, the [[Varkey Foundation]] and [[Populus Ltd|Populus]] conducted an international study examining the attitudes of 20,000 people aged 15 to 21 in twenty countries.{{refn|Survey included people born between 1995 and 2001, which includes two years of Millennials.|name=first|group=note}}{{refn|Countries studied in 2016 Varkey Foundation-Populus international study: Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Israel, Italy, Japan, New Zealand, Nigeria, Russia, South Africa, South Korea, Turkey, the U.K., and the U.S.|name=second|group=note}}<ref name=":7">{{Cite news |last=Weale |first=Sally |date=8 February 2017 |title=UK second only to Japan for young people's poor mental wellbeing |url=https://www.theguardian.com/society/2017/feb/08/uk-second-japan-young-people-poor-mental-wellbeing |access-date=18 April 2018 |work=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> The survey showed that 66% of people aged 15 to 21 favored legal [[abortion]], but there was significant variation among the countries surveyed: support for this procedure was strongest in France, the United Kingdom, and Canada, but lowest in Argentina, Brazil, and Nigeria.<ref name=":8">{{Cite news |last1=Broadbent |first1=Emma |last2=Gougoulis |first2=John |last3=Lui |first3=Nicole |last4=Pota |first4=Vikas |last5=Simons |first5=Jonathan |date=January 2017 |title=Generation Z: Global Citizenship Survey |url=https://www.varkeyfoundation.org/media/4487/global-young-people-report-single-pages-new.pdf |access-date=November 15, 2019 |publisher=[[Varkey Foundation]]}}</ref> [[Gallup (company)|Gallup]] polls conducted in 2020 in the U.S. revealed that 61% of people aged 18 to 29—older members of Generation Z and younger Millennials—considered themselves [[Abortion-rights movements|pro-choice]], while only 34% identified as [[Anti-abortion movements|pro-life]]. In general, the older someone was, the less likely that they supported access to abortion.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019 |title="Pro-Choice" or "Pro-Life," 2018 Demographic Table |url=https://news.gallup.com/poll/244709/pro-choice-pro-life-2018-demographic-tables.aspx |access-date=November 16, 2019 |website=Gallup}}</ref> Nevertheless, anti-abortion sentiments among American youths in the early 2020s were sufficiently strong to motivate them to participate in the annual [[March for Life (Washington, D.C.)|March for Life in Washington D.C]].<ref name=":02">{{Cite news |last=Morrow |first=Brendan |date=January 23, 2020 |title=Young anti-abortion marchers look forward to 'post-Roe America' |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/jan/23/young-anti-abortion-marchers-washington-march-for-life |access-date=January 24, 2020 |work=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Mullen |first1=Michelle |last2=Lai |first2=Man Sum |date=January 22, 2022 |title=Gen Z marchers praying for an end to US abortion |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/av/world-us-canada-60088680 |access-date=January 25, 2022 |work=BBC News}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Paz |first=Christian |date=January 24, 2022 |title=The Anti-abortion Movement's Gen-Z Victors |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2022/01/march-for-life-abortion-protest/621349/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20220124185546/https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2022/01/march-for-life-abortion-protest/621349/ |archive-date=January 24, 2022 |access-date=January 25, 2022 |work=The Atlantic |department=Politics}}</ref>

Following the [[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization|overturning of Roe v. Wade]] in 2022, 65% of men  and 71% of women aged 18 to 29 in America supported legal abortion in "most or all cases". However, in the 2024 presidential election, only 43% of Gen Z men said that abortion was a "critical issue".<ref>{{cite web |title=Abortion Attitudes in a Post-Roe World: Findings From the 50-State 2022 American Values Atlas |url=https://www.prri.org/research/abortion-attitudes-in-a-post-roe-world-findings-from-the-50-state-2022-american-values-atlas/ |website=prri.org |publisher=PRRI |access-date=26 April 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Abortion Attitudes in a Post-Roe World: Findings From the 50-State 2022 American Values Atlas |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2024/aug/20/abortion-rights-dobbs-men |website=[[The Guardian]] |access-date=26 April 2025}}</ref>

=== Gender equality and LGBT rights ===
{{Further|Generation Z and LGBT}}[[File:Youths'_Views_on_Same-sex_Marriage_(2016).png|394x394px|right]]
The 2016 Varkey Foundation and Populus survey also asked about people's viewpoints on moral questions regarding [[Biological sex|sex]] and [[gender]]. Overall, 89% supported [[Gender equality|equality between men and women]], with support being the highest in Canada and China (both 94%), and the lowest in Japan (74%) and Nigeria (68%). 74% favored recognizing [[transgender rights]], but with large national differences, from an overwhelming majority of 83% in Canada to a bare majority of 57% in Nigeria. 63% approved of [[same-sex marriage]], but there were again huge variations among countries. 81% of young Germans and 80% of young Canadians agreed that same-sex couples should be allowed to marry, compared to only 33% of young Turks and 16% of young Nigerians who did.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":8" /> In a 2018 Pew Research Center survey, 48% of Generation Z participants said that same-sex marriage was good for society.<ref name=":60" />

=== Civil liberties ===
[[File:Students march because Black Lives Matter (17130711447).jpg|thumb|260x260px|[[Minneapolis]] students participate in a school [[walkout]] to protest [[police brutality in the United States]], [[Black Lives Matter#2015|2015]].|left]]{{See also|Intersectionality|Woke}}
A 2020 Politico survey showed that American voters aged 18 to 23 support the [[Black Lives Matter]] movement to a greater extent (68%) than all registered voters (54%), and support police much less (39%) than all registered voters (66%).<ref name=":2" /> While Democrats of all ages generally agree that black people are treated unfairly in the United States at equal rates (roughly 80%), Gen Z [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]] agree at much greater rates (43%) than millennial Republicans (30%) or older generations (20-23%).<ref name=":60" /> Gen Z also supported protesters and protests more than registered voters by a 12% margin, and were more likely to view protesting as an effective way to make political change.<ref name=":2" />

In a worldwide Deloitte survey, 60% of Generation Z say that [[Institutional racism|systemic racism]] is widespread in society. Over two in ten also reported that they felt discriminated against "all the time", with this number rising to three in ten among [[Sexual minority|sexual minorities]], and four in ten among [[ethnic minorities]].<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |date=2021 |title=Deloitte 2021 Global Millennial and Gen Z Survey Report |url=https://www2.deloitte.com/content/dam/Deloitte/global/Documents/2021-deloitte-global-millennial-survey-report.pdf |access-date=September 5, 2021 |website=[[Deloitte]]}}</ref>

A 2016 Varkey Foundation and Populus survey found that, worldwide, young people's support for [[Freedom of speech|free speech]] dwindled if it was deemed offensive to a religion (56% support) or a minority group (49%).<ref name=":8" />

== Economic values ==
Generation Z is much more likely to turn to their parents for financial advice than Millennials.<ref name="Brown-2019">{{Cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2019/07/16/savings-parents-say-its-embarrassing-to-rely-on-them-after-27/1705355001/|title=Gen Z, millennials: It's 'embarrassing' to rely on parents for money after 27|last=Brown|first=Dalvin|date=July 16, 2019|work=USA Today|access-date=July 23, 2019}}</ref> Unlike their predecessors, members of Generation Z are more cautious of developing financial debt and many are already saving for retirement. Their money-saving habits are reminiscent of those who came of age during the Great Depression. In the second quarter of 2019, the number of people from Generation Z carrying a credit card balance increased by 41% compared to that of 2018 (from 5,483,000 to 7,746,000), as the first wave of this demographic cohort became old enough to take out a mortgage, a loan, or to have credit-card debt, according to [[TransUnion]].<ref name="Tuchscherer-2019" /> The financial industry expects continued growth in credit activity by Generation Z, whose rate of credit delinquency is comparable to those of the Millennials and Generation X.<ref name="Tuchscherer-2019">{{Cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2019/08/18/credit-cards-report-gen-z-taking-more-debt/2008655001/|title=As they reach adulthood, Gen Z isn't shying away from credit cards, loans and other debt|last=Tuchscherer|first=Rebekah|date=August 18, 2019|work=USA Today|access-date=August 27, 2019}}</ref> According to a 2019 report from the financial firm [[Northwestern Mutual]], student loans were the top source of debt for Generation Z, at 25%. For comparison, mortgages were the top source of debt for the Baby Boomers (28%) and Generation X (30%); for the Millennials, it was credit card bills (25%).<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2019/09/18/student-loans-are-not-the-no-1-source-of-millennial-debt.html|title=Millennials have an average of $28,000 in debt—and the biggest source isn't student loans|last=Leonhardt|first=Megan|date=September 18, 2019|work=CNBC|access-date=October 30, 2019|department=Become Debt-free}}</ref>
[[File:Bernie Sanders and crowd at UNC-Chapel Hill.jpg|thumb|250x250px|Bernie Sanders, a self-described [[Democratic socialism|democratic socialist]], speaks at [[UNC-Chapel Hill]] for his 2020 presidential campaign, 2019.]]
Generation Z views [[socialism]] more positively than previous generations, especially in the United States. In a 2018 Gallup poll, 51% of Americans aged 18 to 29—young Millennials and older Gen Z—have a positive view of socialism, compared to 45% having a positive view of [[capitalism]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |date=2018-08-13 |title=Democrats More Positive About Socialism Than Capitalism |url=https://news.gallup.com/poll/240725/democrats-positive-socialism-capitalism.aspx |access-date=2021-06-21 |website=Gallup.com |language=en}}</ref> In a 2019 poll by YouGov and [[Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation]] found that more than half of Gen Z Americans have an unfavorable view of capitalism, and almost two-thirds said they were likely to vote for a socialist candidate.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=Kight |first=Stef W. |date=October 28, 2019 |title=70% of millennials say they'd vote for a socialist |url=https://www.axios.com/millennials-vote-socialism-capitalism-decline-60c8a6aa-5353-45c4-9191-2de1808dc661.html |access-date=2021-06-22 |website=Axios |language=en}}</ref> Much of this shift has been attributed to [[Bernie Sanders]]'s [[Bernie Sanders 2016 presidential campaign|2016]] and [[Bernie Sanders 2020 presidential campaign|2020]] presidential campaigns.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" /> Additionally, according to the 2020 [[Edelman (firm)|Edelman]] Trust Barometer, 57% of those ages 18 to 34 worldwide say that modern-day capitalism "does more harm than good", though this figure roughly corresponds with all other age groups.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020 |title=Edelman Trust Barometer 2020 |url=https://www.edelman.com/sites/g/files/aatuss191/files/2020-01/2020%20Edelman%20Trust%20Barometer%20Global%20Report_LIVE.pdf |access-date=September 5, 2021 |website=[[Edelman]]}}</ref>

Though still generally popular among all age groups, Europeans ages 18 to 29 are less likely than older groups to support [[Redistribution of income and wealth|fiscal redistribution]].<ref name=":6" /> This age group in the EU is also more likely to attribute poverty to “laziness or lack of willpower", though this sentiment is not the majority view of the cohort in most countries in Europe.<ref name=":6" />

According to a 2021 Forefront Market Research poll commissioned by the [[Institute of Economic Affairs]], a conservative think tank, 67% of young people in the UK (those aged 16 to 34) say they would like to live in a socialist economic system. The poll also found that overwhelming majorities of Gen Z Britons (aged 16 to 22) blame capitalism for the [[Affordability of housing in the United Kingdom|UK housing crisis]] to some extent, label climate change as a capitalist problem, and would like to [[Nationalization|nationalize]] utilities and railways.<ref>{{Cite web |title=67 per cent of young Brits want a socialist economic system, finds new poll |url=https://iea.org.uk/media/67-per-cent-of-young-brits-want-a-socialist-economic-system-finds-new-poll/ |access-date=2022-07-31 |website=Institute of Economic Affairs |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Niemietz |first=Kristian |date=July 2021 |title=LEFT TURN AHEAD? Surveying attitudes of young people towards capitalism and socialism |url=https://iea.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Left-turn-ahead.pdf |access-date=July 31, 2022 |website=Institute of Economic Affairs}}</ref>

According to a 2018 [[International Federation of Accountants]] survey of G20 countries, the top three public policy priorities for members of Generation Z are the [[Economic stability|stability of the national economy]], the quality of education, and the availability of jobs. The bottom issues, on the other hand, were addressing [[Economic inequality|income and wealth inequality]], making regulations smarter and more effective, and improving the effectiveness of [[international taxation]]. Moreover, [[Health care|healthcare]] is a top priority for Generation Z in Canada, France, Germany, and the United States. Tackling wealth and income inequality is deemed of vital importance in Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2019 |title=Identifying What Matters Most to the Next Generation |url=https://www.ifac.org/system/files/uploads/PPRAG/IFAC_GenZ_Report_FINAL.pdf |access-date=July 10, 2019 |website=International Federation of Accountants}}</ref>

== International affairs ==
Polling has shown that Generation Z is, on the whole, less nationalist than previous generations, a shift stemming in part from increased contact with other cultures.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Yglesias |first=Matthew |date=26 June 2019 |title=The youngest American adults are the least nationalistic |url=https://www.vox.com/2019/6/26/18759774/generation-z-morning-consult-poll |access-date=2022-12-20 |website=Vox}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dharma |first1=Ni Made Muthiara |last2=Dharmapurusa |first2=Avanindra Amrtani |last3=Nathanael |first3=Kevin |last4=Pandin |first4=Moses Glorino Rumambo |date=n.d. |title=Challenges of Generation Z in Maintaining Local Culture As a National Identity in Globalization Era |url=https://jptam.org/index.php/jptam/article/view/2694 |journal=Jurnal Pendidikan Tambusai |volume=5 |issue=3 |pages=10708–10720 |doi=10.31004/jptam.v5i3.2694 |doi-broken-date=July 12, 2025 |issn=2614-3097}}</ref><ref>Jurášková, Olga, et al. "Differences in the Expected Contribution of Higher Education in the Millennials Generation and the Generation Z." ICERI 2016 Proceedings (2016).</ref>

In 2019, [[Harvard Institute of Politics|Harvard University's Institute of Politics]] Youth Poll asked voters aged 18 to 29 – younger Millennials and the first wave of Generation Z – what they would like to be priorities for US foreign policy. They found that the top issues for these voters were countering terrorism and protecting human rights (both 39%), and protecting the environment (34%). Preventing nuclear proliferation and defending U.S. allies were not as important to young American voters.<ref name=":83">{{Cite web |date=April 22, 2019 |title=Spring 2019 Harvard IOP Youth Poll Results |url=https://iop.harvard.edu/about/newsletter-press-release/spring-2019-harvard-iop-youth-poll-results |access-date=September 14, 2019 |website=Harvard Kennedy School Institute of Politics}}</ref>  According to the [[Eurobarometer]] in 2016 to 2018, over 60% of Europeans between 15 and 24 viewed [[globalization]] positively, in stark contrast with older cohorts.<ref name=":6" />

A 2018 YouGov poll asked British voters whether [[Brexit|leaving]] the [[European Union]] was a good idea in hindsight. They found that 42% said yes while 45% said no. Among them, 19% of those between the ages of 18 and 24 said yes, as did 61% of pensioners. Overall the British public has not changed their minds on the issue<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Eatwell |first1=Roger |title=National Populism - The Revolt Against Liberal Democracy |last2=Goodwin |first2=Matthew |publisher=Pelican Book |year=2018 |isbn=978-0-241-31200-1 |location=Great Britain |chapter=Chapter 10: Towards Post-populism}}</ref> as this aligned with the results of the [[2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum|2016 Brexit referendum]] when younger voters were more likely to vote to stay in the European Union.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Moore |first=Peter |date=June 27, 2016 |title=How Britain voted at the EU referendum |url=https://yougov.co.uk/topics/politics/articles-reports/2016/06/27/how-britain-voted |access-date=February 17, 2021 |website=YouGov |language=en-gb}}</ref>

=== Immigration ===
[[File:Youths'_Views_on_Legal_Migration.png|503x503px|right]]
In a 2016 Varkey Foundation and Populus international survey,{{refn|Countries studied in 2016 Varkey Foundation-Populus international study: Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Israel, Italy, Japan, New Zealand, Nigeria, Russia, South Africa, South Korea, Turkey, the U.K., and the U.S.|name=second|group=note}} the question of whether or not those 15 to 21 favored legal migration received mixed responses. Overall, 31% believed their governments should make it easier for immigrants to work and live legally in their countries while 23% said it should be more difficult, a margin of 8%.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":8" /> While 72% of Brazilian youths thought their government was doing too little to address the international [[European migrant crisis|refugee crisis]], only 16% of young Turks did; in the U.K. that number was 48%.<ref name=":7" />

A [[YouGov]] poll conducted in the spring of 2018 revealed that 41% of Britons between the ages of 18 and 24 thought that immigration to their country was "too high", compared to 58% of those 25 to 49.<ref name=":32" />

===Gaza war===
{{See also|Gaza war protests|Gaza war protests at universities}}
Members of Generation Z are more likely to support [[Palestine (region)|Palestine]] and oppose [[Israel]] than any other generation.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Muchnik |first1=Jordan |last2=Kamarck |first2=Elaine |date=9 November 2023 |title=The generation gap in opinions toward Israel |url=https://www.brookings.edu/articles/the-generation-gap-in-opinions-toward-israel/ |access-date=2 January 2024 |website=Brookings}}</ref> According to an October 2023 NPR/PBS NewsHour/Marist National poll which surveyed 1,313 U.S. adults, 48% of [[Millennials]] and Generation Z said that the U.S. government should publicly voice support for Israel, compared to 63% of [[Generation X]], 83% of the [[baby boomers]], and 86% from the [[Silent Generation|Silent]] and [[Greatest Generation]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The generation gap in opinions toward Israel |url=https://www.brookings.edu/articles/the-generation-gap-in-opinions-toward-israel/ |website=Brookings}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=14 October 2023 |title=New Poll Shows Americans Strongly Support Israel, but Generational, Racial Divides Are Wide |url=https://www.kqed.org/news/11964499/new-poll-shows-strong-american-support-for-israel-amid-generational-racial-divides |website=KQED |language=en-us}}</ref> In December 2023, More in Common conducted a survey among British citizens from various age groups. Generation Z respondents were the most likely to consider Hamas to be freedom fighters and the least likely to consider Hamas a terrorist organisation.<ref name=":13">{{Cite web |date=4 December 2023 |title=More than Choosing Sides |url=https://www.moreincommon.org.uk/media/bujj4fjp/more-than-choosing-sides-more-in-common-report-december-2023.pdf |access-date=2 January 2024 |website=More in Common |page=26}}</ref>

== Environmentalism ==
{{See also|School strike for climate}}
[[File:20240625 Global warming across generations - warming stripes.svg |thumb |Global warming—the progression from cooler historical temperatures (blue) to recent warmer temperatures (red)—is being experienced disproportionately by younger generations. With continued fossil fuel emissions, that trend that will continue.<ref name="GW_generations">{{Cite web |date=22 March 2023 |title=Warming Across Generations |url=https://www.climatecentral.org/climate-matters/warming-across-generations |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240613055205/https://www.climatecentral.org/climate-matters/warming-across-generations |archive-date=13 June 2024 |publisher=Climate Central}}
* Data source for [[Global surface temperature|global average surface temperature]]: {{cite web |title=Global temperature / Global mean temperature |url=https://climate.metoffice.cloud/temperature.html |publisher=Met Office (Meteorological Office, UK ) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240117053030/https://climate.metoffice.cloud/temperature.html |archive-date=17 January 2024 |date=2024 |url-status=live}} (scroll down to Berkeley Earth under Global Mean Temperature)
* [[Warming stripes]] concept by [[Ed Hawkins (climatologist)|climatologist Ed Hawkins]]</ref>]]
Generation Z is more likely than other generations to believe that [[climate change]] is real and to support [[climate change mitigation]]. Polling from 2018 of Americans over the age of 13 by Pew suggested that 54% of Generation Z believed that climate change is real (making them the second-most likely cohort to do so) and is due to human activities, while only 10% [[Climate change denial|reject]] the [[scientific consensus on climate change]].<ref name=":60" />

A worldwide Deloitte survey saw that climate change and protecting the environment top Generation Z's primary concerns, with curbing unemployment and expanding health care access not far behind.<ref name=":10" />

[[File:Greta Thunberg (48882847963).jpg |thumb |In 2018, [[Greta Thunberg]] began to inspire worldwide protests for greater action against climate change.]]
A 2019 poll of over 10,000 internet users aged 18 to 25 years old in 22 countries around the world found that 41% of responders believed that climate change was one of the most important issues facing the world, the most popular response. The second-most common problem cited was environment-related pollution at 36%. Top priorities on a national level differed but environmental concerns also polled relatively strongly in this category.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Barbiroglio |first=Emanuela |date=9 December 2019 |title=Generation Z Fears Climate Change More Than Anything Else |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/emanuelabarbiroglio/2019/12/09/generation-z-fears-climate-change-more-than-anything-else/ |access-date=2021-05-29 |website=Forbes |language=en}}</ref> A 2020 survey conducted for [[Newsround]] of Britons aged 8 to 16 suggested that 80% of young Generation Z viewed climate change as a problem, with more than a third thinking it was "very important". 58% of respondents worried about the impact that climate change would have on their future. 19% said they faced nightmares about the topic whilst 17% said it had affected their eating and sleeping habits.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Climate anxiety: Survey for BBC Newsround shows children losing sleep over climate change and the environment |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/newsround/51451737 |access-date=2021-04-19 |work=CBBC Newsround |language=en-GB}}</ref> 41% of respondents did not trust adults to properly address the crisis.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2020-03-03 |title=One in five UK children report nightmares about climate change |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/climate-change-children-idUSL1N2AV1FF |access-date=2021-04-19 |work=Reuters |language=en}}</ref> Addressing climate change is very important for Generation Z in India and South Korea.<ref name=":0" /> In contrast, less than 20% of Europeans aged 15 to 24 viewed climate change as a top 2 challenge facing the EU according to the Eurobarometer.<ref name=":6" />

One of the earliest political movements primarily driven by Generation Z was [[School Strike for Climate]] in the late 2010s. The movement saw millions of young people around the world, inspired by the activities of Swedish teenage activist [[Greta Thunberg]], protest for greater action on climate change.<ref name="BusinessInsiderClimate">{{Cite web |last=Luce |first=Ivan De |date=20 September 2019 |title=12 Gen Zers who skipped school to march across New York for the Global Climate Strike share why this is the most urgent issue of their generation |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/global-climate-strike-gen-zers-share-their-thoughts-2019-9 |access-date=2021-05-30 |website=Business Insider |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Keegan |first=Hannah |date=2019-12-17 |title=Greta Thunberg's effect on youth action on the climate crisis |url=https://www.stylist.co.uk/people/profile-greta-thunberg-school-strike-climate-change-global-warming-activist-time/336784 |access-date=2021-05-30 |website=Stylist |language=en}}</ref>

== Other views ==

=== Uncertain future ===
A 2024 study on Generation Z in Spain found that pessimistic economic expectations shape preferences for populist parties.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zagórski |first=Piotr |last2=Roch |first2=Juan |last3=Tudó-Cisquella |first3=Julià |last4=López-Yagüe |first4=Alberto |last5=Cordero |first5=Guillermo |date=May 2025 |title=Generation Z: pessimistic and populist? A conjoint experiment on the determinants of populist voting in Spain |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/european-political-science-review/article/generation-z-pessimistic-and-populist-a-conjoint-experiment-on-the-determinants-of-populist-voting-in-spain/215F0C4849F0FF32AC0798C4F51BCE62 |journal=European Political Science Review |language=en |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=202–220 |doi=10.1017/S1755773924000237 |issn=1755-7739}}</ref> This effect was mediated by ideology, as young pessimists on the left tend to be attracted by anti-elitism, while those on the centre-right are drawn to people-centrism. A 2025 study of adolescents (aged 16–21) in the UK and Greece explored the link between "future anxiety"—defined as pessimism and uncertainty about the future—and political attitudes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Borghi |first=Olaf |last2=Niraki |first2=Melina |last3=Seremeta |first3=Ermioni |last4=Smets |first4=Kaat |last5=Tsakiris |first5=Manos |date=2025-10-10 |title=Facing a dark future: Young people's future anxiety and political attitudes in the UK and Greece |url=https://advances.in/psychology/10.56296/aip00042/ |journal=advances.in/psychology |language=en |volume=2 |pages=e555124 |doi=10.56296/aip00042 |issn=2976-937X}}</ref> While researchers found that young women reported higher levels of future anxiety than young men in both countries, the political implications of this anxiety showed notable gender differences. Among young men in both the UK and Greece, higher future anxiety was associated with more right-conservative ideological self-classification. In the UK sample, this link was further pronounced: young men with higher future anxiety also showed greater support for authoritarian principles and less actively open-minded thinking. Among young women, these associations between future anxiety and right-conservative ideology or authoritarianism were not credibly different from zero. The authors suggested that future anxiety may be a relevant correlate of the emerging ideological gender gap, noting that ideological differences between the genders were most apparent among participants reporting high levels of future anxiety.

=== Trust in institutions ===
In 2019, the Pew Research Center interviewed over 2,000 Americans aged 18 and over on their views of various components of the federal government. They found that 54% of the people between the ages of 18 and 29 wanted larger government compared to 43% who preferred smaller government and fewer services. Older people were more likely to pick the second option.<ref>{{Cite news |date=October 1, 2019 |title=Public Expresses Favorable Views of a Number of Federal Agencies |url=https://www.people-press.org/2019/10/01/public-expresses-favorable-views-of-a-number-of-federal-agencies/ |access-date=January 4, 2020 |work=Pew Research Center |department=U.S. Politics & Policy}}</ref>

According to a 2018 survey by Pew Research Center, 70% of Generation Z want the government to play a more active role in solving their problems.

However Gen Z's trust in institutions may have seen a large decrease: In the Fall 2024 Harvard Youth Poll, only 11% of those ages 18–29 felt that the United States is “generally headed in the right direction,” and a 2023 poll by the American Public Media Research Lab found that only 27% of Americans ages 18–25 “agree strongly” that democracy is the best system of government, compared with 48% for all ages.<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 9, 2024 |title=Gen Z doesn't believe in government. The solution is closer to home than you think. |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/opinion/voices/2024/12/09/local-government-elections-gen-z-vote/76794946007/ |first=David|last=Millman |access-date=December 13, 2024 |work= USA Today |department=U.S. Politics & Policy}}</ref>

=== Gun ownership ===
{{quote box
| quote = "The people in the government who are voted into power are lying to us ... And us kids seem to be the only ones who notice and are prepared to call B.S."
| author = [[X González]]
| source = February 18, 2018, in [[Fort Lauderdale]]<ref name="NYTimes-GonzalezLeadsStudentOutcry-2018">{{Cite news |last=Bailey |first=Jason M. |date=February 18, 2018 |title=Emma González Leads a Student Outcry on Guns: 'This Is the Way I Have to Grieve' |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/02/18/us/emma-gonzalez-florida-shooting.html |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref>
| align = right
| width = 35%
}}The [[March for Our Lives]], a [[2018 United States gun violence protests|protest taking place in the aftermath]] of the [[Stoneman Douglas High School shooting]] in 2018 was described by various media outlets as being led by students and young people. Some even describe it as the political "awakening" of Generation Z or that these protesters were "the voice of a generation on gun control".<ref>* {{cite news|last1=Wierson|first1=Arick|date=23 March 2018|title=March for our Lives gun control rally only hints at the political power of Generation Z|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2018/03/23/march-for-our-lives-gun-control-rally-only-hints-at-the-political-power-of-generation-z.html|access-date=24 March 2018}}
* {{cite news|last1=Anapol|first1=Avery|date=14 March 2018|title=NJ student march organizers pen op-ed to NRA We Wont Let You Win|work=The Hill|url=https://thehill.com/blogs/blog-briefing-room/378333-nj-student-march-organizers-pen-op-ed-to-nra-we-wont-let-you-win/|access-date=24 March 2018}}
* {{cite news|date=13 March 2018|title=Dear National Rifle Association: We Won't Let You Win. From, Teenagers.|work=New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/03/13/opinion/nra-shooting-marjory-stoneman-douglas.html|access-date=24 March 2018}}
* {{Cite web |last=Wallheiser |first=Mark |date=February 20, 2018 |title=What's different now? Parkland students won't let us get away with no action on guns. |url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/news-columns-blogs/fabiola-santiago/article201179124.html |access-date=June 9, 2019 |website=Miami Herald}}</ref>

In a 2019 Rasmussen poll, US Gen Z and Millennial respondents supported stricter gun laws at the highest rates—68%. Majorities of older generations also agreed.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Poll: Gen Z Spurs Shift in Voter Support for Gun Control {{!}} RealClearPolitics |url=https://www.realclearpolitics.com/articles/2019/08/15/poll_gen_z_spurs_shift_in_voter_support_for_gun_control__141014.html |access-date=2021-09-05 |website=www.realclearpolitics.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Voters Want More Gun Control But Admit Mass Shootings Can't Be Stopped |url=https://www.rasmussenreports.com/public_content/politics/current_events/gun_control/voters_want_more_gun_control_but_admit_mass_shootings_can_t_be_stopped |access-date=2021-09-05 |website=www.rasmussenreports.com |language=en}}</ref> In a 2017 poll, Pew found that among the age group 18 to 29, 27% personally owned a gun and 16% lived with a gun owner, for a total of 43% living in a household with at least one gun. Nationwide, a similar percentage of American adults lived in a household with a gun.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Parker |first1=Kim |last2=Horowitz |first2=Julianna Menasce |last3=Igielnik |first3=Ruth |last4=Oliphant |first4=J. Baxter |last5=Brown |first5=Anna |date=June 22, 2017 |title=America's Complex Relationship With Guns |url=https://www.pewsocialtrends.org/2017/06/22/americas-complex-relationship-with-guns/ |access-date=November 13, 2019 |work=Pew Research Center |department=Social Trends}}</ref>

=== COVID-19 pandemic ===
{{See also|Doomscrolling}}
According to a worldwide Deloitte survey, 69% of those in Gen Z reported that they took their government's public health guidelines seriously during 2020. Members of Generation Z surveyed also feel that they are doing more than others in their countries to limit the spread of [[COVID-19]].<ref name=":10" />
